title: Rush Hour 3
full_review:
The Eiffel Tower at night has never looked more spectacular in a motion picture. But until "Rush Hour 3" (New Line) gets there, the dour Chief Inspector Lee (Jackie Chan) and frantic, wisecracking detective James Carter (Chris Tucker) suffer comedic death by a thousand cuts from Parisian cliches staler than a 4-year-old box of "Freedom Fries."

Director Brett Ratner and screenwriter Jeff Nathanson, who both made "Rush Hour 2," keep the car chases taut and lovingly choreograph the swordplay, gunplay and martial arts. But six years after the second installment, the rapport between the two leads is forced, Chan seems tired, and the best of the comedy, when not resorting to a slapstick twirl with a giant in a kung fu studio, looks borrowed from the "Naked Gun" spoofs.

In this installment, Lee and Carter, who reunite in Los Angeles, fight a secret crime syndicate called the Triads. From the first film, Nathanson brings back Chinese ambassador Han (Tzi Ma) and his daughter, now 20, Soo Yung (Jingchu Zhang). Han is shot as he attempts to uncover the Triads before the World Criminal Court, Lee finds out the assassin is Kenji (Hiroyuki Sanada), his "brother" from their orphanage, Soo Yung is abducted, and the key evidence of the syndicate's existence turns out to be in Paris.

There, Lee and Carter encounter (quelle surprise!) scruffy French taxi driver George (Yvan Attal), who secretly longs to be an international spy ("The guns! The shooting! Now I know what it is to be an American!") and becomes their eager compatriot.

There's a sadistic police chief (Roman Polanski, in a surprising cameo), an obligatory dip into the Parisian sewers, and evidence hidden with sultry nightclub singer Genevieve (Noemie Lenoir) and Varden Reynard (Max von Sydow), the elegant head of the World Criminal Court, who may not be on the side of justice.

The potpourri of culture clashes also includes the unbilled Judith Ivey as Sister Agnes, a nun who calmly translates -- and paraphrases -- the rants of a Triad bad guy Carter raucously interrogates, without losing either her dignity or her deft comic timing.

The Eiffel Tower becomes a versatile jungle gym for the final showdown. And Carter's shrill, scattershot quips and occasional breaks into song propel the film as if Tucker knows his career depends on it. But when he launches into "Everybody Was Kung Fu Fighting" after dispatching a roomful of villains, it's clear this franchise has lurched to a close.

At a brisk 86 minutes, the film contains nearly bloodless violence, crude and crass language, skimpy female costuming, implied female nudity, implied sexual activity, mild sexual banter and innuendo. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
